newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand downgrade impact on earnings seen slight.
newsitem.headline: Thailand downgrade impact on earnings seen slight.

text.p: Thailand's downgraded sovereign and bank debt ratings will raise future foreign funding costs for Thai borrowers but analysts said on Thursday they would produce little short-term impact on bank and corporate earnings.

Analysts said repercussion from Moody's Investors Service's decision to lower Thai ratings mostly had been absorbed in advance by the market before the agency downgraded them to A3 from A2 on Wednesday.

"The Moody's downgrades have already been priced into a lot of Thai debt instruments which have carried higher yields in the past few months," said Mike Stead, head of research at Union Securities Co Ltd.
The Moody's move was preceded by a warning in February when the rating agency put Thai long-term ratings on review for possible downgrades.

When a borrower is downgraded by a ratings agency it usually means investors will demand higher yields on the borrower's bonds. In the long-term, this will mean borrowers having to pay -- hence the impact on corporate earnings, analysts said.
Moody's cut Thailand's foreign currency ceilings for bonds and bank deposits to A3 from A2. It also cut senior debt and deposit ratings of five Thai banks to the same investment grade rating.

It said the downgrades reflected concern over the asset quality of Thai banks and the instability of a Thai financial system shaken by exposure to a prolonged slump of a troubled Thai property sector.

Bankers and analysts estimated that foreign funding costs of Thai bank and corporate borrowers had earlier risen by up to 40 basis points (bps) after Moody's cut short-term Thai debt rating in September.
A basis point is one one-hundreth of a percentage point.
Another foreign analyst said the Moody's downgrades would raise Thai foreign funding costs over time with corporate borrowers taking the brunt of the increased burden.

"The downgrades puncture market confidence to a degree...but it is extremely difficult to quantify the (extent) of higher funding costs...it is not a foregone conclusion that banks would face higher funding costs in the near term," he said.

Traders in New York said price talk on the 30-year tranche of Thailand's $500 Yankee bond issue centred around 110 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, up from 75-80 bps when it was first planned early this year.
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan is leading a roadshow on the bond issue in major U.S. cities this week.

The analysts said Thai money market liquidity had risen in the past month due to sluggish loan demand because of a dramatically slowing economy and increased money supply resulting from the recent launch of government pension and provident funds.
Prateep Leelakittikul of Hongkong and Shanghai Bank said downgraded Thai banks may have to pay an extra five basis points of foreign funding costs because of the Wednesday downgrades.
But Prateep agreed with most analysts that local Thai lending rates would not rise.

"The interest rate outlook is pretty static now. Banks are cautious in lending out fresh loans, private business could not shoulder high funding cost while the Bank of Thailand wants high interest rates to help its defence of the baht," he said.
Thai prime lending rates are among the highest in the region, averaging 13.25-13.75 percent.
Analysts said the impact of higher funding costs was moderated by a recent shift of majority bank funding from foreign loans to local sources.
Stead estimated that major Thai banks currently relied on foreign borrowing for only 10-20 percent of total funding.
"It is a slippery slope of argument that the downgrades would force banks to other sources of funding," said another foreign analyst who declined to be named.
He also cautioned against excessive negative views on Thailand, saying its downgraded ratings were still on the same level as Hong Kong's.
